explainedBy: An investor slumps at his workstation as a breakout collapses, introducing the necessity of the core selling rule.

storyboard.claim: Breakouts sometimes fail, necessitating an uncompromising exit rule.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps at his workstation desk looking worried as a breakout pattern fails.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the warning in beat 222 that even perfect chart patterns can fail.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the immediate personal disappointment of a failed breakout before the rule is stated.

explainedBy: The disciplined institutional manager explains survival while the amateur investor slumps in defeat.

storyboard.claim: Cutting losses is where professionals survive and amateurs lose everything.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager in an office addresses the amateur retail investor who slumps beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts professional longevity with retail destruction introduced in beat 223.
storyboard.addedInformation: Juxtaposes the surviving professional with the devastated amateur side by side.

explainedBy: An investor sits alone late at night illuminated only by his brokerage workstation.

storyboard.claim: A retail investor sits alone at night staring at a losing position in a beloved company.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An investor sitting alone at his trading workstation in the dim glow of his screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the narrative scenario illustrating the emotional torment of taking a loss.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes the lonely, solitary environment where retail emotional battles take place.

explainedBy: The seated investor stares anxiously at his screen as his favorite stock registers a 7% drop.

storyboard.claim: A favorite stock with a perfect chart has dropped 7% below the purchase price.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor remains seated at his desk, his face tensing with worry as the 7% loss displays.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the nocturnal desk scenario, revealing the exact 7% deficit on the monitor.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the shift from neutral study to acute emotional distress as the loss hits the trigger.

explainedBy: The investor hesitates with his hand reaching toward the mouse as fear and ego urge him not to sell.

storyboard.claim: The investor hesitates to sell because ego promises the stock will bounce back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor stays at the workstation, hand reaching hesitantly toward the controls with an afraid expression.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the sequence from recognizing the loss to the frozen hesitation before the sell button.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the psychological freeze where personal ego battles trading discipline.

explainedBy: The investor rationalizes the drop as temporary, desperate to avoid making the loss permanent.

storyboard.claim: Rationalizing a loss as a temporary dip is an ego defense to avoid acknowledging a mistake.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The seated investor holds a hand to his head in agonizing thought while the rationalization is struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the sequence of inner monologue trying to justify holding the losing stock.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike-through directly discredits the seductive lie that the drop is merely temporary.

explainedBy: The seated investor closes his eyes in numb focus, rejecting the instinct to cling to the trade.

storyboard.claim: Cutting a loss requires tuning out the instinct that tells you not to lock in a deficit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits motionless at the workstation with a blank, closed-off expression confronting the truth.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Advances the sequence to the moment of mental detachment right before execution.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts the blank sensory detachment required to override visceral financial panic.

explainedBy: The investor clicks the sell button with firm determination, executing the hardest order in trading.

storyboard.claim: Clicking the sell button and swallowing pride is the most difficult physical action in investing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor firmly points downward to click the order execution, his expression resolving into neutral discipline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the 6-beat night workstation sequence with the decisive execution of the sale.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the breakthrough moment where discipline overcomes emotional paralysis.

explainedBy: The institutional manager points firmly to the protective shield representing the ironclad 7% to 8% loss cutoff rule.

storyboard.claim: Every single loss must be cut at 7% to 8% below purchase price without exception.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager in his office points decisively toward a protective shield icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the individual desk scenario to the universal protective loss-cutting rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Positions the stop-loss rule visually as an active defensive shield protecting trading capital.

explainedBy: The investor firmly rejects external news, analyst upgrades, and excuses for holding a falling stock.

storyboard.claim: There are no exceptions, news checks, or analyst upgrades that justify delaying a loss cut.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor gestures firmly with an uncompromising angry stance at the trading desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reenforces the unyielding nature of the 7-8% shield rule declared in beat 231.
storyboard.addedInformation: Displays active resistance against the common temptations to rationalize a losing trade.

explainedBy: A flow diagram links the strict 8% maximum loss cutoff directly to the 20% profit target.

storyboard.claim: An 8% maximum loss pairs with a 20% to 25% profit target to form a disciplined risk framework.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-node flow diagram showing '8% Loss' leading into '20% Profit'.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects the loss prevention rule to its profit-taking counterpart.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clarifies the structural pairing of asymmetric risk and reward in O'Neil's strategy.

explainedBy: The institutional manager highlights the power of systematically locking in 20% gains.

storyboard.claim: Taking profits systematically at 20% provides the high-yield side of the trading equation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager points authoritatively with a knowing smirk in an abstract financial space.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the mathematical demonstration of asymmetric risk-reward.
storyboard.addedInformation: Presents the institutional confidence behind routine mathematical gain-taking.

explainedBy: The investor expresses surprise at the realization that a 7% cutoff allows being wrong 66% of the time.

storyboard.claim: Cutting losses at 7% allows an investor to be wrong on two out of every three trades.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor speaks with genuine surprise as the mathematical asymmetry is stated.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pairs the 20% win with the 7% loss cutoff to show the astonishing margin for error.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the eye-opening realization that perfection is unnecessary when losses are truncated.

explainedBy: A flow diagram maps how a 33% win rate combined with a 7% loss cutoff guarantees account survival.

storyboard.claim: A 33% win rate combined with strict 7% stops mathematically guarantees trading survival.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step flow diagram connecting '33% Wins' through '7% Loss' to 'Survival'.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Synthesizes the mathematical proof from beats 234 and 235 into a complete survival mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Diagrams the mathematical certainty that triumphs over emotional anxiety.

explainedBy: The frustrated investor confronts the institutional manager about the agonizing reality of being stopped out.

storyboard.claim: In practice, cutting losses can feel infuriating when stocks immediately bounce back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor vigorously gestures in frustration while the institution listens impassively.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from abstract mathematical perfection to the practical emotional grievance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the active debate between real-world frustration and mathematical theory.

explainedBy: The investor describes following the rules precisely to sell at an 8% loss.

storyboard.claim: An investor follows the rule, cuts at 8% down, and feels disciplined yet vulnerable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor continues explaining the painful scenario, hands held out to describe the exit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Builds the first half of the common whipsaw dilemma.
storyboard.addedInformation: Details the initial compliance with the rule before the whipsaw occurs.

explainedBy: The investor slumps in misery at selling the bottom while the manager acknowledges the feeling.

storyboard.claim: Selling right before a 20% bounce makes the disciplined trader feel like a complete fool.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps in total dejection beside the calm portfolio manager who smiles knowingly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the punchline of the pushback scenario: getting whipsawed out at the exact bottom.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the acute humiliation of following rules only to watch the stock rebound.

explainedBy: The institutional manager reminds the shaken retail trader to examine the catastrophic alternative.

storyboard.claim: Getting shaken out happens repeatedly, but the alternative of holding losses is far worse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager addresses the worried investor directly, gesturing toward the bigger picture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts the perspective from short-term embarrassment to systemic survival.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames whipsaw losses as the minor trade-off against catastrophic portfolio wipeout.

explainedBy: The manager holds O'Neil's historical reference book citing IBM's 1926 violent shakeout.

storyboard.claim: William O'Neil points to IBM in 1926 as a classic example of a violent shakeout in a winning stock.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager holding a reference book in his office, citing historical precedents.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces historical evidence to prove that shakeouts happen even to the greatest market leaders.
storyboard.addedInformation: Anchors the discussion in empirical market history rather than theoretical speculation.

explainedBy: The professional explains that disciplined traders swallow their pride and re-enter at a higher buy point.

storyboard.claim: Professionals swallow their pride and rebuy a shaken-out stock when it crosses the pivot again.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager points upward decisively, demonstrating re-buying at higher prices.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the professional reaction to a stock that recovers after triggering a stop loss.
storyboard.addedInformation: Demonstrates the counter-intuitive mastery of paying up rather than pouting.

explainedBy: The retail investor reacts with amazement as the manager explains why professionals hold no grudges.

storyboard.claim: The market does not know you exist, so holding an emotional grudge against a stock is foolish.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor gestures in astonishment while the fund manager calmly explains emotional neutrality.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts retail spite with institutional objectivity following a stopped-out trade.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stresses the complete absence of personal vendettas in professional trading.

explainedBy: The investor holds a protective shield, understanding that small losses are merely insurance premiums.

storyboard.claim: An 8% loss is not an analytical error but a necessary insurance premium for capital preservation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor stands in an abstract space holding a golden protective shield with calm acceptance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the psychological pain of the loss into a deliberate defensive expense.
storyboard.addedInformation: Transforms the perception of a loss from failure to prudent risk management.

explainedBy: The investor ponders at his workstation the looming danger of a stock that never recovers.

storyboard.claim: Eventually, a stock that drops 8% will not bounce back, turning into a disastrous collapse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor stands at his desk with a worried expression as the bounce assumption is struck down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the insurance premium in beat 244 must be paid every single time.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shatters the complacency that every declining stock will eventually recover.

explainedBy: The investor slumps in terror beside a crash icon as catastrophic 50% to 80% losses wipe out capital.

storyboard.claim: Without the 8% rule, a single stock dropping 50% to 80% can wipe out an entire account.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps in fear beside a dramatic crash icon representing market ruin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the catastrophic endpoint that the 8% insurance rule exists to prevent.
storyboard.addedInformation: Illustrates the true ruinous danger of refusing to take small losses.

explainedBy: The investor aggressively confronts his own ego, committing to cut losses before pride destroys capital.

storyboard.claim: Reversing retail instinct requires ruthlessly suppressing ego to cut losses before pride destroys capital.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail trader stands in an abstract space with intense, angry determination.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Synthesizes the psychological victory required to survive the market crashes of beat 246.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts the fierce internal war against ego required for professional execution.

explainedBy: The fund manager emphasizes that counter-intuitive loss cutting is required for market survival.

storyboard.claim: Cutting losses immediately is unnatural to human psychology but mandatory for long-term survival.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The portfolio manager stands calmly in his office, emphasizing the core survival mandate.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the loss-cutting doctrine before pivoting to the framework's core vulnerability.
storyboard.addedInformation: Affirms that market survival depends on embracing unnatural, disciplined habits.

explainedBy: The investor points to the CAN SLIM framework with concern, acknowledging it is not a magic bullet.

storyboard.claim: CAN SLIM is not an invincible magic bullet that works in every market condition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor points in an abstract analytical space with a worried expression as 'magic bullet' is struck.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from praising the system's power to examining its specific vulnerabilities.
storyboard.addedInformation: Temples uncritical enthusiasm by highlighting systemic limitations.

explainedBy: The institutional manager explains that knowing when a trading strategy fails is vital.

storyboard.claim: Understanding the precise market conditions where a system fails is as important as knowing how it works.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager speaks thoughtfully in his office, breaking down system mechanics.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reinforces the necessity of stress-testing the CAN SLIM methodology.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames failure analysis as an essential component of professional competence.

explainedBy: A spectrum diagram identifies the choppy whipsaw bear market as the lethal environment for CAN SLIM.

storyboard.claim: The fatal vulnerability of momentum breakouts is a choppy, rangebound whipsaw bear market.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum continuum ranging from 'Bull Trend' to 'Whipsaw' with the indicator near maximum chop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pinpoints the exact market environment where breakout systems encounter distress.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the structural shift from trending conditions to choppy algorithmic traps.

explainedBy: The seated investor gets stopped out at 7% as a cup-with-handle breakout fails in a weak market.

storyboard.claim: Buying breakouts in an indecisive market leads to immediate failure and a 7% stop-out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits at his workstation looking anxious as the first breakout trade fails.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the repetitive sequence showing how whipsaws bleed trader capital.
storyboard.addedInformation: Demonstrates that textbook technical patterns collapse when the broader tide is negative.

explainedBy: The investor slumps at his desk as another stock breakout fails, triggering another 7% loss.

storyboard.claim: A second breakout fails the following week, triggering another 7% loss despite perfect discipline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps further over the workstation monitors as a second loss registers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the whipsaw sequence, showing repetition of the loss-cutting cycle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the grinding erosion of capital and morale from repeated stop-outs.

explainedBy: The investor clutches an emptying wallet in distress after five consecutive stop-outs bleed his capital.

storyboard.claim: Repeatedly taking 7% losses in a whipsaw market inflicts death by a thousand cuts on trading capital.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits at his workstation holding a depleted wallet with an expression of fear.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Culminates the whipsaw sequence by exposing the devastating cumulative impact of repeated stops.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows that even flawless rule execution drains an account if trading in the wrong market.

explainedBy: The institutional manager points to a navigational compass representing Market Direction, the crucial 'M'.

storyboard.claim: The system is only vulnerable to whipsaws if the trader ignores Market Direction, the M in CAN SLIM.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager in his office points toward a crisp navigational compass icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the whipsaw trap to the navigational rule that prevents it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces market direction as the macro compass that overrules individual stock setups.

explainedBy: The portfolio manager explains that CAN SLIM is specifically engineered to exploit sustained bull markets.

storyboard.claim: CAN SLIM is engineered specifically to compound wealth during sustained bull market uptrends.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager speaks warmly and confidently in his trading office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the true intended operational environment for CAN SLIM momentum strategies.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clarifies that the system is a specialized offensive weapon, not an all-weather tool.

explainedBy: Beside a chess knight strategy icon, the manager declares that true discipline means stepping aside.

storyboard.claim: In a choppy or bear market, the highest discipline is to stop trading rather than taking repeated losses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager stands beside a chess knight game icon, gesturing to step away.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides the tactical remedy to the death-by-a-thousand-cuts whipsaw dilemma.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes inaction not as giving up, but as a superior strategic decision.

explainedBy: The investor sits patiently at his workstation holding physical cash, completely removed from market risk.

storyboard.claim: The ultimate discipline during market chop is holding 100% cash and refusing to force trades.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor sits peacefully at his workstation holding a coin, charts left inactive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the concept of stopping the game into the concrete posture of holding cash.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts sitting in cash as an active, deliberate position of strength.

explainedBy: The seated investor struggles with the restless anxiety of doing nothing while holding cash.

storyboard.claim: Doing absolutely nothing is psychologically the hardest challenge for an active retail trader.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor remains seated with his cash, an expression of restless anxiety creeping onto his face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explores the psychological resistance to staying in cash introduced in beat 258.
storyboard.addedInformation: Exposes the internal itch to gamble that torments disciplined traders in cash.

explainedBy: The investor battles the compulsive impulse to reach toward the keyboard and enter sub-par setups.

storyboard.claim: The psychological urge to feel productive drives traders out of cash and into dangerous, low-quality setups.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor leans forward in his chair, hand reaching temptingly toward trading controls in agitation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Demonstrates how the boredom identified in beat 259 transforms into reckless trading.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the physical temptation that destroys trader discipline during market lulls.

explainedBy: The institutional manager instructs the retail trader to keep his capital dry until the market tide turns.

storyboard.claim: Mastery consists in preserving capital in cash until institutional accumulation confirms a new uptrend.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager and retail trader stand side by side in the office in calm mutual alignment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes chunk 7 by uniting retail patience with institutional market timing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Harmonizes retail behavior with institutional market currents.
